name: jerryscript
desc: Ultra-lightweight JavaScript engine for the Internet of Things
why: Tiny JavaScript engine built for microcontrollers, a curious look at how far a language can be squeezed down.

brief.what_it_is: JerryScript is a JavaScript engine written in C99, aimed at microcontrollers and other very constrained devices. The homepage says it can run with only a few kilobytes of RAM (under 64 KB) and under 200 KB of ROM. It takes JavaScript source, or precompiled snapshots of it, and executes it on the device. The homepage also says it can access peripherals from JavaScript. The brew formula installs a `jerry` executable.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a JavaScript engine for resource-constrained devices such as microcontrollers, for the Internet of Things, where a full engine is too large.
brief.how_it_works: The README says it is heavily optimized for low memory use and offers snapshot support for precompiling JavaScript source to byte code. It is a C library with a C API meant to be embedded in applications, and the README describes it as having a mature API. The README does not explain the internals beyond this.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew, the README's route is to clone the repository and build with Python (python tools/build.py). Building from source needs Python and a C99 toolchain, though the README does not list specific versions. For embedding, the docs cover configuration (docs/01.CONFIGURATION.md) and the port API (docs/05.PORT-API.md). I did not see any account or hardware requirement beyond a target device for the constrained use case.
brief.standout: The engine is claimed to fit under 64 KB RAM and 200 KB ROM and to build to about 258K for ARM Thumb-2. The README also notes that snapshot support lets source be precompiled to byte code, which suits devices that cannot parse JavaScript cheaply at runtime.
brief.status: unknown. The README and homepage give no release date, version number, or last-commit date. It has a GitHub Actions CI badge and an active-looking documentation set, but I could not confirm recent activity from what I fetched.
brief.caveats: The README says full ECMAScript 5.1 compliance but only 70% of ECMAScript 2025, so newer JavaScript features are partial. The homepage's ROM figure (<200 KB) and the README's 258K binary size for Thumb-2 are not obviously the same measurement, so check the exact build configuration before quoting either. The community chat link points to freenode, which may be outdated. The project accepts only Apache 2.0 licensed contributions signed under a Developer's Certificate of Origin. Licence is Apache 2.0.

judge.reason: A JavaScript engine squeezed into microcontroller-scale memory is a genuinely surprising way to explore language runtimes and embedded computing.

entry.title: JerryScript
entry.tldr: A JavaScript engine written in C99 that is meant to run in under 64 KB of RAM on microcontrollers, with a `jerry` command for trying it on a desktop.
entry.deeper_look:
JerryScript is a JavaScript engine for devices where a normal engine will not fit. The homepage says it can run with under 64 KB of RAM and under 200 KB of ROM. It takes JavaScript source, or precompiled snapshots of it, and executes it. The homepage also says it can reach peripherals from JavaScript. Brew installs a single executable, `jerry`.

The project exists for the Internet of Things. The README describes it as "a lightweight JavaScript engine for resource-constrained devices such as microcontrollers" and says it is "heavily optimized for low memory consumption". It is a C library with a C API, meant to be embedded in other programs, and the README calls that API mature.

The idea underneath is snapshots. Parsing JavaScript is costly for a tiny chip, so the source can be compiled to byte code ahead of time on a bigger machine. The device then loads and runs the byte code only. This turns a dynamic language into something closer to a firmware blob.

The language coverage is a trade-off too. The README claims full ECMAScript 5.1 compliance and about 70% of ECMAScript 2025. That makes it a good way to see which parts of JavaScript you can drop and still have a working language.
entry.install:
brew install jerryscript

# Running it on a real microcontroller needs a target device.

entry.whats_unique: Most JavaScript engines are built for speed on big machines. This one is built to fit in kilobytes, and it can precompile scripts to byte code so the device never has to parse source.
entry.caveats: The brief could not confirm recent release or commit activity, and ES2025 support is only partial at about 70%.
